messages.title: Requests, responses and conversation history
messages.brief: A request is information our program sends to a service. A response is what comes back. A tool request inside that response asks our program to do something; it is not the result of doing it.
messages.example: The model asks for get_machine_spec with CONV-3. Python runs that function. The returned record becomes a tool message with the matching tool_call_id. The next model request includes this exchange.

functions.title: Functions, inputs and returned results
functions.brief: A function is a named piece of code. Arguments are the inputs given to it. return gives a result back to the caller. Printing a value only puts it on the screen.
functions.example: get_machine_spec("CONV-3") receives one identifier and returns a dictionary. The calling program can read that dictionary before choosing another step.

records.title: Dictionaries and small Python classes
records.brief: A dictionary stores named values, such as status and data. A class groups related values and operations. A dataclass helps define a small record without writing all the setup code yourself.
records.example: An Observation keeps id, tool, arguments and result together. obs.result["status"] reads one named field; it does not decide whether the entire task is finished.

copies.title: Why a saved record needs its own copy
copies.brief: Two variables can refer to the same mutable object. If we save only another reference, a later change can also change what appears to be our history. A deep copy gives nested dictionaries and lists their own stored values.
copies.example: Save a result containing a list, then change that original list. The observation should still show what the tool returned at the time we saved it.

conditions.title: Conditions, loops and return
conditions.brief: An if statement chooses a branch. A while loop repeats its body. return leaves the current function. None can mean that a function has no stopping reason to report yet.
conditions.example: If steps is already at max_steps, stop_reason returns "max_steps". If no limit has been reached, it returns None and the caller may continue.

validation.title: Valid data and the right data
validation.brief: Validation checks whether data follows the rules we specified. Some rules check its shape and types. Others check whether it belongs to this particular task. Passing one kind of check does not automatically pass the other.
validation.example: CONV-7 can be a correctly written machine identifier while still being wrong for a task about CONV-3.

time.title: Timeouts and elapsed time
time.brief: A timeout limits how long we wait for one operation. A whole-run budget limits how long the overall attempt should continue. We need both because a loop counter cannot interrupt an operation that never returns.
time.example: A limit of six decisions does not help if the first tool call hangs. The local tool subprocess also needs a timeout.

record.hint1: Look at the fields in Observation and the existing State.log method. Which inputs must the new record keep?
record.hint2: Make an ID from the next position, deep-copy arguments and result, append the Observation, log the event and return the Observation.
record.explanation: record stores what happened. Its deep copies protect the record from later changes. The ID lets a report refer back to one observation. It does not decide whether that observation completes the task.
record.rubric: Explain why the inputs and result are copied, where the Observation is appended, and why recording is separate from verification.

verify.hint1: Which evidence does each goal require? The matching helpers will supply suitable observations once you also complete the small input guard.
verify.hint2: Build a mapping of found evidence, choose the required names from the goal, and list missing names. A report with zero query rows also needs nonempty readings. Return the associated IDs and facts.
verify.explanation: verify expresses the task checklist. It uses matched observations rather than model confidence. Different goals need different evidence, and an empty query cannot support a percentage report.
verify.rubric: Explain the required evidence for report versus readings, how missing controls ready, and why evidence IDs identify actual matched observations.

stats_inputs.hint1: Read obs.arguments. Which two named inputs should come from the saved query and specification?
stats_inputs.hint2: Build the expected argument dictionary from values and limit. Compare the whole dictionary, including every list value; a count or summary comparison is not enough.
stats_inputs.explanation: statistics_inputs_match connects a calculation to the values and limit collected for this task. Different lists can produce identical summaries. The caller rejects a mismatched input record before checking the returned arithmetic.
stats_inputs.rubric: Explain where values and limit come from, why the full argument dictionary is compared, and why a False return skips this observation even when its summary looks correct.

guards.hint1: Read Config and compare its limits with the counters and elapsed time in State.
guards.hint2: Check the total deadline, step count, reported live-token threshold and enabled no-progress limit in the provided order. Reaching the boundary is enough; return None only if none applies.
guards.explanation: stop_reason reports why another attempt is no longer allowed. It does not claim success. Individual tool attempts and operation timeouts are also bounded by the existing runner.
guards.rubric: Explain an exact boundary, the None return, the special disabled no-progress value and why a stop reason is not verified completion.

loop.hint1: Trace the action through the runner and ask who needs to see its returned observation next.
loop.hint2: Use runner.execute to obtain obs, give obs.result to the same planner, call _update_check on the updated State, and return what the caller expects.
loop.explanation: The helper connects execution to feedback and fresh verification. The runner records the result; the same planner receives feedback; the new check sees the evidence just collected.
loop.rubric: Explain the order execute, observe, update check; distinguish a stored observation from planner feedback and describe why an old check is insufficient.

tasks.title: Why we need a loop
tasks.purpose: Connect the earlier weeks to a task with dependent tool actions.
tasks.logic:
In Week 1, we connected an LLM to a local Python program. You can think of this as giving the program a brain: it could understand a request and produce a response.

In Week 3, we gave it hands. The model could request a tool, and our Python program could run that tool.

But having a brain and hands does not automatically mean the program can finish a whole task.

Here is the task we will work on today: Check CONV-3's temperature readings for 2 March 2026, 10:00 to 10:25 (UTC+08:00). Read its reference limit, calculate the share of readings above that limit, and give a summary we can check.

Before we run anything, think about what we would need to check the final answer. Temperature readings are one part. We also need the reference limit and a calculation that really uses those inputs.
